content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a Prototype-based Global Hardest Example Miner (GHEM) and a Prototype-based Global Triplet Loss (pTriplet)  in the CV and NLP areas. In main focus is on the global hard example instead of local hard example mining. Compared to the existing global hard example mining, the author solves a problem on the outlier anchors and the method to correct them.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The problem found in this paper is interesting. the literature dis not paid attention to the problem of excessively imcompact clusters caused by anchors being outliers.

Weaknesses
1. The writing of the paper is terrible. Please define a new concept/idea and then refer to it. This problem happened in multiple places in the paper:
Section 3 " Second, the global hardest examples are mined from the cluster intersection of these global hardest classes " -> missing evidence to support.
A few lines in the next, "Then, pTriplet combines other losses" -> missing the definition of pTriplet in the early of this section.
A few lines in the next, "..pick the global hardest example set H = {h1, h2, h3, ..., hm}." -> whose hard example?
Section 3.1 
".. located at the intersection between clusters as mentioned in Introduction 1." -> a) Introduction is not used for defining a new concept/idea. b) even in the Introduction, there is no clear illustration or definition of this new concept/idea.

"NNG" in multiple places before its definition at the top of page 5. -> need to define it first

2. Claims of the paper are not well supported and even slightly not correct
a. "It takes the positive examples farthest from the anchor as hard positive examples, both of which have the
same identity." The positive selection has already been explored in the Easy Positive paper[i]. Positive examples farthest from the anchor may not be optimal for the triplet loss. A more extended concern is whether Easy Positive can solve the problem of anchor outlier raised in the paper. 
b. "...eventually resulting in the excessively incompact cluster" incompact cluster may help for generalization of the metric learning, please go over the paper metrics proposed in [ii] and t-SNE in [I].

3. The author tries to find hard examples from a global view. But the concern is if these hard examples from a global view can be some noisy data? Is there any visualization to illustrate it? this evidence will be more supported for the paper.

[i]Xuan, H., Stylianou, A., & Pless, R. (2020). Improved embeddings with easy positive triplet mining. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (pp. 2474-2482).

[ii] Karsten Roth, Timo Milbich, Samarth Sinha, Prateek Gupta, Björn Ommer, and Joseph Paul Cohen. Revisiting training strategies and generalization performance in deep metric learning. In Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, ICML 2020, 13-18 July 2020, Virtual Event, volume 119 of Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, pages 8242–8252, 2020.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The bad writing makes the paper confusing to read and forms in low quality.
content.summary_of_the_review: Please rewrite the draft for the next submission.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper aims at improving the triplet loss by proposing 1) mining approximate global hardest examples and 2) a prototype-based triplet loss. At the beginning of every training epoch, the prototype of each class is computed by averaging the feature vectors of the samples in the class. Then they compute the pairwise distance between the prototypes and propose a heuristic algorithm to find approximate hardest examples for training. On each training iteration, they propose to update the prototype vector by using exponential moving average.

However, the paper does not seem to be finished. It does not introduce how the prototype-based triplet loss is actually defined and how the mined examples are used.

Experiments on person re-identification and few-shot relation extraction tasks suggest that the proposed method leads to marginal improvements compared with the GS method [Liao & Shao 2022].
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths

1) It is quite well motivated (to find more meaningful triplets to help model training)
2) The related works are discussed quite thoroughly
3) Using prototype to improve the triplet sampling makes sense

### Weaknesses

1) The paper does not seem to be finished. In section 3.2, it seems to be "truncated" after introducing how to update the prototypes during training iterations. It misses how the pTriplet loss is actually defined; how the prototypes / mined examples are involved in the loss; how it is plugged in to the neural network model training, etc.

2) The proposed GHEM algorithm is actually an approximation to finding the global hardest examples. Given that it is only computed at the beginning of each epoch, why we don't just compute the exact pairwise distances between the instances, and then use them to find the exact hardest examples? How good is the proposed approximation? Can we define some metrics to measure this, e.g., among the top-100 exact global hardest examples, how many of them can be mined with the proposed approximation algorithm?

3) Many math formulations are vague or not rigorous. This makes it hard to clearly understand proposes method. For example,
    1) Eq (2), what are the $n_1, n_2, \dots, n_l$? Are they the class ids? They should be $n_{i1}, n_{i2}, \dots$, which depends on $i$, right?
    2) The graph $G$ is defined in Eq (3) but never used afterwards. What's the point of defining the graph? Besides, what does the $H(v_j)$ mean?
    3) The $cos(\cdot)$ function is used in both Eq(5) and Eq(6). However, in Eq(5) it seems to denote the cosine distance, but in Eq(6) it seems to denote cosine similarity?
    4) In Eq(6), the lowercase $p_i$ should be the uppercase $P_i$. It also misses various subscript even if we omit the subscript $i$, e.g., it should be $d_j = 1-cos(P_i, x_j)$, $O = \{o\in S_i | d_j > \lambda \}$, $N = \{n\in S_i | d_n <= \lambda\}$.
    5) In Eq(7), the superscript can be confused with raising to a power. Better to be written as something like $P_i^{(t)}$.


4) In section 4.6, it is claimed that without GHEM and pTriplet, the performance drops sharply. But according to the Table 5 and 6, the metric drops are arguably marginal. How to justify the "sharp drop"? Is the improvement statistically significant enough? How can we tell it is a solid improvement rather than just "overfitting" to the test set, given that no validation set is used in both tasks and the algorithms could be tuned based on the test performance?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**. As elaborated above, the math formulations are vague or not rigorous. The clarity needs to be improved.

**Quality**. The high-level idea makes sense. But the paper misses quite many details and the experiments may not well justify the improvements, as elaborated in the weaknesses above.

**Novelty**. The proposed method is extended from several existing work -- the graph-based sampler from [Liao & Shao 2022], the prototype-based update algorithm could be traced back to [Wen et.al. 2016], [a], and [b]. The paper has its novel contribution but relatively marginal.

**Reproducibility**. The paper includes implementation details in the supplementary materials. But the method introduction is not complete as elaborated in the weaknesses. It can be hard to fully reproduce the results.

[a] Prototypical networks for few-shot learning. NeurIPS 2017
[b] Joint Detection and Identification Feature Learning for Person Search, CVPR 2017
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper is not finished and not polished. Due to missing some introduction to the core pTriplet loss and many vague / not rigorous math formulations, the readers will not be able to fully understand the paper based on its current version. Thus, I would recommend a reject.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a hard example mining method for triplet loss. Based on the assumption that constructing mini-batch with harder negative examples results in better performance, it defines samples in the boundary region between an anchor and its nearest class as the hardest negatives. In addition, it detects and corrects outlier anchors for better loss computation. Experiments show that the method improves the existing hard negative mining methods and baseline random sampling methods on within and cross-domain person re-identification and few-shot relation extraction tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

- The method improves the baseline hard example mining baselines for two tasks, person re-identication and few-shot relation extraction.
- The method improves mAP as well as rank-1 recall, which reflects the overall representation quality.
- The method is evaluated under various settings and shows better generalization performance compared to the baselines under the cross-domain settings.

Weakness

- The paper assumes that constructing triplets using harder negative examples enhances the feature representation. However, this assumption is not validated. There are also existing observations that employing semi-hard negatives achieved better accuracy than employing the hardest negatives [A]. Will the method work better if the harder examples are selected, for example, by reducing delta? If harder examples do not always lead to better performance, what is the proper balance between hardness and diversity of negatives?

- Effectiveness of each proposed component can be analyzed better by comparing with proper baselines or upperbounds. For GHEM, compared to the hardest examples found by brute force search, how effective the samples are in terms of both compute cost and hardness? What is the advantage over an existing baseline to train classifiers together and choose the samples with largest losses [B,C]? Experimental comparison will also be necessary.

- This paper also assumes that the simple average between two class centers are the boundary. However, I am not sure if this will hold when the amount intra-class variation changes a lot across classes. For example, if the intra-class variation is large for the anchor class and is small for the negative class, then the samples around the middle point of two class centers will likely from the anchor class. Also, since the method averages all samples of each class to get the proxy, such proxy can be noisy when there are outliers, which makes the class relation graph and nearest class selection less reliable.

- Experimental validation is not sufficient. One strong baseline of metric learning is the cross entropy loss (or joint cross entropy and the metric learning loss), because CE loss makes supervision based on global distribution rather than local relations. Does the method still improves the baseline under such condition? Comparison with other existing global hard example mining methods [D,E] look missing.
The cross-dataset accuracy
- Accuracy improvements look a bit marginal compared to the baselines (Table 1-3).

- It is good that the method is evaluated under both person ReID and FSRE tasks. However, I am still not sure if the method will improve the baselines for larger-scale settings such as face retrieval.

- Analysis
Training dynamics can be studied to understand the model training procedure better. How do the nearest (hardest) classes for anchors change over the iteration? I guess the nearest classes can converge to specific ones after initial epochs of training, which may potentially cause overfitting by sampling negatives only from a limited number of classes. How does the training and validation accuracy change over training? Does the model overfit if trained longer? Have any related issues been observed?
There are several hyper-parameters for hard sample mining and anchor correction. However, their effects are not well studied in the experiments. More analysis is necessary. How do they affect the performances? Do they sensitive to datasets choices (i.e., tasks and sample distributions)?
Also, it would be good to discuss computational complexity and scalability.


[A] FaceNet: A Unified Embedding for Face Recognition and Clustering, CVPR 2015
[B] Doppelganger mining for face representation learning, ICCV Workshop 2017
[C] How to train triplet networks with 100k identities?, ICCV Workshop 2017
[D] Stochastic Class-based Hard Example Mining for Deep Metric Learning, CVPR 2019
[E] Bag of Negatives for Siamese Architectures, BMVC 2019
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written. However, I could not find novel findings in the paper due to lack of analysis as stated above.
Some important details, such as mini-batch construction algorithm, triplet construction from mini-batch, loss formulation, and batch size look missing. So, I am not sure about its reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review:
In summary, the paper proposes a novel hard example mining method for the triplet loss, but I could not find new findings or insights.

---
I thank the authors for the answer. After reading the answer, I would like to keep my rating.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studies the hard example mining problem in metric learning. Particularly, the paper proposed to locate the global hardest examples and correct outlier anchors  based on class prototypes. Accordingly, a prototype-based triplet loss is developed 
to alleviate the influence of the outlier anchor and provides a normal anchor for Triplet Loss. Extensive experiments on both generalized person re-identification and few-shot relation extraction tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed protype-based triplet loss.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. This paper presents a prototype-based triplet (pTriplet) loss to alleviate the influence of the outlier anchor and provides a normal anchor for Triplet Loss. Particularly, the pTriplet loss includes two parts, i.e., prototype-based global hardest example mining and prototype-based outlier anchor correction.
2. Extensive experiments on two tasks of different fields, i.e., person re-identification and few-shot relation extraction, are conducted, which demostrates the effectiveness of the proposed pTriplet loss.
	
Weakness:
1. The concept of cosine distance seems misused. In Eq. (5), the reviewer suppose it was $1-\cos(f(x_s), M)$.
2. The sensitivity of hyper-parameters in the proposed method are not specified and discussed, e.g., $\delta$ in Eq. (5), $\lambda$ in Eq. (6) and $\alpha$ in Eq. (7), $\beta$ in Eq. (8). These hyper-parameters determine the effectiveness of the proposed method. 
3. Many concepts are vague. This makes it hard to clearly understand the proposed method, for exmaple, 1) $n_i$ in Eq. (2) denotes class id or a set of class samples? 2) In Eq.(5), $I$ denotes a set of examples that should be a set  $\mathbb{I}$
4. Some assumptions are not rigorously verified. For example, the authors assume that samples neear the mid-point of two protypes are hardest samples. 
5. The authors try to find the outlier anchor using the protypes and correct them. The outliers are assumed as noise which will pull away the prototype. So, why do we keep these outliers? If these outliers can be identified, why do not delete these outliers instead of correct them? 
6. There are some typos and format problems, for example, 1) the citation format in Introduction, 2) lambda --> $\lambda$ in Eq. (6); 3) "We take the sphere with m" --> $M$
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The motivations of this paper are clearly illustrated. It is somewhat novel. However, there are still some vague and unrigorous parts required further description and discussion. Due to some key hyper-parameters are not specified in the paper,  the main results are difficult to be reproduced.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper introduces a global hardest example mining method with prototype-based triplet loss. The idea of the method is somewhat novel and the experiments show the effectiveness of the proposed methods. However, there are some vague and logical problems need further explanation and discussion.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
